title: Bhagavad Gītā — Core Teachings
description: Test your understanding of the essential teachings of the Bhagavad Gītā — karma, dharma, ātmā, and the nature of Brahman.

questions.question: Who narrated the Bhagavad Gītā to Dhṛtarāṣṭra during the Kurukṣetra war?
questions.explanation: Sañjaya, minister to Dhṛtarāṣṭra, was granted divine vision by Vyāsa to see the battle and narrated the Gītā to the blind king.
questions.shloka: धृतराष्ट्र उवाच | धर्मक्षेत्रे कुरुक्षेत्रे समवेता युयुत्सवः |
questions.transliteration: Dhṛtarāṣṭra uvāca | dharma-kṣetre kuru-kṣetre samavetā yuyutsavaḥ |

questions.question: Kṛṣṇa tells Arjuna that the ātmā (soul) can be destroyed by weapons.
questions.explanation: Kṛṣṇa explicitly states: 'nainaṁ chindanti śastrāṇi' — weapons cannot cut the soul. It is eternal, unborn, and indestructible.
questions.shloka: नैनं छिन्दन्ति शस्त्राणि नैनं दहति पावकः |
questions.transliteration: nainaṁ chindanti śastrāṇi nainaṁ dahati pāvakaḥ |

questions.question: Who am I?
clues: I was born from a pot, not a womb.
I was the preceptor of both the Pāṇḍavas and the Kauravas.
I faced my own son on the battlefield of Kurukṣetra.
questions.explanation: Droṇācārya was born from a pot (droṇa), taught both Pāṇḍavas and Kauravas, and his son Aśvatthāmā fought alongside him on the Kaurava side.

questions.question: Which of the following are among the 18 chapters (adhyāyas) of the Bhagavad Gītā?
questions.explanation: 'Vedānta Yoga' is not a chapter in the Gītā. The 18 chapters include Sāṅkhya Yoga (Ch.2), Karma Saṁnyāsa Yoga (Ch.5), Vibhūti Yoga (Ch.10), and Mokṣa Saṁnyāsa Yoga (Ch.18).

questions.question: Who spoke these words: "Yato dharmastato jayaḥ" — Where there is dharma, there is victory?
questions.context: Spoken at the conclusion of the Mahābhārata
questions.explanation: Sañjaya speaks these final words of the Bhagavad Gītā narrative, concluding his report to Dhṛtarāṣṭra.

questions.question: Arrange these events from the Bhagavad Gītā in the correct order:
items: Arjuna sees his relatives arrayed for battle and despairs
Kṛṣṇa begins teaching with Sāṅkhya — the nature of the ātmā
Arjuna declares he will not fight and puts down his bow
questions.explanation: Order: (1) Arjuna surveys the battle and despairs seeing relatives, (2) puts down his bow, (3) Kṛṣṇa begins with Sāṅkhya teachings on the soul, (4) reveals Viśvarūpa in Chapter 11.

questions.question: Read the Assertion and Reason below:
questions.assertion: Kṛṣṇa instructs Arjuna to perform his duty as a Kṣatriya and fight.
questions.reason: According to the Gītā, action performed without attachment to results is the highest form of yoga.
options: Both A and R are true — R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true — R does NOT correctly explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.explanation: Both statements are true. Kṛṣṇa does urge Arjuna to fight as his svadharma, and the principle of naiṣkarmya (acting without attachment to fruits) is the core of Karma Yoga — which directly supports why Arjuna should act.

questions.question: Match each Bhagavad Gītā chapter with its correct yoga:
questions.explanation: Ch.2 = Sāṅkhya Yoga, Ch.3 = Karma Yoga, Ch.6 = Dhyāna Yoga (Ātma Saṁyama Yoga), Ch.12 = Bhakti Yoga.

questions.question: Which of these is the odd one out among the mahāvākyas (great sayings) of the Upaniṣads?
options: Tat Tvam Asi — That thou art
Dharmo Rakṣati Rakṣitaḥ — Dharma protects those who protect it
questions.explanation: 'Dharmo Rakṣati Rakṣitaḥ' is from the Manusmṛti, not an Upaniṣadic mahāvākya. The four mahāvākyas come from the four Vedas (Aitareya, Chāndogya, Bṛhadāraṇyaka, and Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣads).

questions.question: A soldier is ordered to fight in a war he personally believes is unjust, yet his nation and commander depend on him. Which Bhagavad Gītā teaching most directly applies?
questions.scenario: Modern dilemma: duty vs. personal moral conviction
options: Naiṣkarmya — complete renunciation of all action
Svadharma — fulfilling one's own duty, even if imperfect, over another's duty
Mokṣa — seek liberation and abandon all worldly roles
Karma-phala — focus only on the results of action
questions.explanation: Kṛṣṇa teaches: 'śreyān svadharmo viguṇaḥ paradharmāt sv-anuṣṭhitāt' — it is better to perform one's own duty imperfectly than another's duty well (BG 3.35). The soldier's svadharma as a protector is the applicable principle.
